lines: {name}.
You came on the Sunday train. She said you would. Then she stopped saying anything.
There are bones walking her fence line. Put them down and I will give you her key. Space swings. I would do it myself, but look at me.
You heard singing in the tunnel and your telephone died in your hand. I am the ordinary part of today.
The bones are still walking the fence. She would have done it herself, once.
It is in your log. Check it. Things that are not written down here do not always stay true.
Good. Before nine, if you can. The bell is at nine.
Not in the house. Not in the cellar. I can smell the rest of the county from this step, and she is not in that either.
Closer than that. Bones first.
You can stop checking on me. I am a dog on a step.
Still a dog. Still a step.
You keep coming back to look. That is a city habit. Making sure the thing is where you left it.
I am not a city dog, {name}. A city dog would have run the first night the lamps went out.
I stayed and counted them going.
Fourteen. Do not count them yourself. It is a different number if you count.
If you must stand there, stand on the left. The right-hand board knows when someone is on it.
It is not looking at you. It is looking at the road behind you, and it has been for some time.
Nothing. There is nothing on the road. I checked, and now you do not have to.
Go inside, {name}. It is later than it looks.
Down. Good.
The house key was always for you. She left fruit. She left a bench. She left a note that tells some of the truth.
There is a bed. Sleep in it. If you die out there you wake in the last place you rested, and it is a long walk back. Do not ask how I know.
Pansy on your fingers. You made one.
She was a witch, {name}. A kind, gentle one. So are you. I would rather you heard it from me than from a mirror.
There are rats under the house, down the hatches in the kitchen. Bring me three pieces of meat.
It is not for me. I have standards.
Three. Keep them.
Meat keeps, where it is going. You will not need it for a while, and I will tell you when you do.
The mine is at the end of the mine road out of Castle. Its mouth is the one with the lamp. A man called Gnox Goldskin dug it and then the dead kept digging.
There is a page missing from this house. The Headmaster confiscates things, and he has never once given anything back at the end of term.
Broken stairs want wood. There is some in the cellar storage, behind a plain lock.
You smell like rust and old gold. Good.
Eat something.
That brass key came out of the vault. It is the Museum's, across the river from Castle, on the road over the bridge. Open until nine.
One wing has had its name painted over. It said MAGIC. You will want to see what they kept under the paint.
Plaster in your hair. You found the wing.
The old families took a little of the gold, for the bench, and left the rest in the hill. That was the whole of the arrangement. Then somebody bought the hill.
The green tag is for the gate of Butterfly Forest. The road to it goes past the ruined library, and the library comes first.
There is one page left in there worth reading. Nothing in that forest will grow for you until you have read it.
You were counted out. Good. Not everybody is.
The cases on his wall had trades on them. Those were county people, the ones who were still well when the nights got long. They were sent where it was still a garden.
I did.
She did. It was the kindest place she had, and it was a garden then.
The Works are past the graveyard. The Factory is the Company's, and the Company kept a key there to a door of its own.
There is a grate at the edge of Castle. The pipes under it run to the Works, dry most days. It is a better road than the one the night shift walks.
You smell of hot wire.
Keep that key on you. It is the Company's own, and it opens one door in the county.

The burial is past Castle, off the graveyard road: the one that goes north, toward the School. Do not go as far as the School. A footpath from the graveyard goes to a stone that says DO NOT, and the Company's key unlocks the stair under it.
The meat from under the house: soak it in Stranglethorn, water and snakeroot, at a bench. The small snakes down there cannot be fought. They can be fed.
The torches down there are blue and they only wake for cold. What burns is in the garden. The big snake keeps its own room and never stops moving. Hit the tail if you cannot reach the head.
Whatever is under that stone was buried with the county's gold, all of it, cast into one ball. Bring the ball up.
You found him, then. Gnox Goldskin, with his arms round it.
She is not dead, {name}. I would know.
The stair behind him goes up, not out. It comes up in the School. The key on the caretaker's bin opens the front doors from outside.
That window has been lit since before you came, and somebody up there rings the bell at nine. Go and see who. Take the ball.
You went up, and you came down again. Not everybody has.
She held it over the county for as long as anyone could have. Longer. What happens to the ball now is yours to say.
There is a train on Sunday. The county still turns. Walk.
Rose and stone. Grey, and it does not settle. That is right.
There were six on the shelf by the door. Then there were none, and then there was only the door.
Lily and gold dust make the next one. There were lilies on that shelf as well.
You went and counted. I did ask.
Twelve, thirteen, fifteen. Yes. Fourteen was there the night Pell went up the road to it with his ladder. I watched him go. I did not watch him come back.
You went and counted. I did ask.
Twelve, thirteen, fifteen. Yes. Fourteen was there the night Pell went up the road to it with his ladder. I watched him go. I did not watch him come back.
You told the stone fourteen. That was kind or it was careless. Out here they come to the same thing, {name}.
I am listening for her. It is a full-time job.
Dear {name}. Happy birthday. I am your aunt Julie. Please come and visit me next week.
I have drawn you a map. It was right when I drew it. Enjoy your birthday. - Julie
The paper is a hundred years old. The ink is not. The map ends at a house and a dog, and the road it shows is not quite the road you walked.
{name}, if you are reading this I am late, not lost.
The bench is set. Gold dust, a vial of water, a pansy from the pantry chest. Make it before you go down any stairs.
The hatches are only the cellar. The orb by the stove is cold on purpose. Touch it. You will not be surprised for long. - J
Gold dust, water, pansy. Stand at the bench, open your bags. The orb by the stove is cold on purpose. - J
THE OTHER WAY OUT. The keys are in the chest at the first stair: the hatch chalked KEYS, by the stove.
Under it, smaller: a cellar with one way out is a mistake you make once. - J
Nothing on the desk. The dust is even all over it but for one clean ring, the size of the stand the orb sits on in the kitchen.
The ring is sharp at the edge. Whatever stood here was taken away since the last time anyone dusted, and nobody has dusted since.
A tin bowl by the step, licked clean. The label on its side is in the same hand as the letter.
DOG. Twice a day. It will tell you if you forget.
It is colder than the room. Then it is colder than you.
Something you always had puts its hand up.
Just glass now.
The only page left in the book. The person buried here loved nature and was a gardener, and the garden burned anyway.
The words are still warm.
Ash.
GOLDSKIN MINING Co. CLOSED. No entry. No exit either, some nights.
DO NOT. Underneath, smaller, scratched later: he took the ball down with him. leave it there.
CASTLE HALT. Trains Sundays only. For Castle, the station road and then the Castle road.
The station road is lit from half past six. Passengers are asked to keep to it, whichever way they are walking.
The bed has been made, recently and badly, by someone without the hands for it.
You sleep. Nothing wakes you. When you open your eyes the blanket has been pulled up.
You sit on the edge until your hands are steady. If it goes badly out there, this is where you will wake.
A fire somebody laid and nobody lit. It catches for you at once.
Nothing comes near while it burns. If it goes badly out there, this is where you will wake.
